title: Memphis
summary: Clashing color, laminate patterns, and toy-like geometry. Postmodern play.
lede: The postmodern style of the Memphis Group, founded in Milan by Ettore Sottsass and active from 1980 to 1987: bright clashing colors, printed laminates, squiggles and speckles, and furniture built from bold, toy-like forms.

era.note: The group’s active years, per Wikipedia. Revivals continue in graphic and web design.

lineage.label: Modernist good design
lineage.note: Memphis rejected the functional restraint associated with the Bauhaus and later modernism.

lineage.label: Studio Alchimia
lineage.note: Sottsass worked with Studio Alchimia, a Milan avant-garde group founded in 1976, before he founded Memphis.

lineage.label: Pop art
lineage.note: Bright commercial color and references to popular culture.

lineage.label: Corporate Memphis
lineage.note: A 2010s flat illustration style named after the group. It shares bright color but not the group’s patterns or furniture forms.

grammar.text: Pink, yellow, turquoise, red, and black together, often at full saturation.
Laminate patterns such as squiggles, speckles, and bacteria-like marks cover whole surfaces.
Cylinders, spheres, arches, zigzags, and stepped forms combine like building blocks.
Parts meet at odd angles and different scales. Symmetry is avoided.
Grid patterns in black and white act as a neutral foil for strong colors.

diagnostic: Four or more saturated colors appear together, including pinks and turquoises.
Repeating patterns such as squiggles, dots, speckles, or grids fill surfaces.
Forms are geometric but playful, with odd combinations of scale and angle.
counter: A restrained palette of one or two colors.
Strict grid alignment and quiet typography carry the design.
Photographic realism or glossy 3D rendering dominates.

confusions.difference: Corporate Memphis is flat vector illustration of people with long limbs. Memphis is about pattern, color, and object form.
Bauhaus shapes are elementary and the palette is primary. Memphis is irregular, decorative, and uses many non-primary colors.
Neo-brutalism also uses bright colors, but relies on thick outlines and hard shadows, not pattern.

do: Combine at least four saturated colors, for example pink, yellow, turquoise, and black.
Fill backgrounds or panels with a pattern: squiggles, confetti dots, or a black-and-white grid.
Place geometric shapes such as circles, half circles, triangles, and zigzags around content, at odd angles.
Use a bold display face for headings and keep body text plain for reading.
dont: Do not put body text on top of a busy pattern. Use a solid panel under text.
Do not use gradients or realistic shadows.
Do not reduce the style to cartoon people. That is Corporate Memphis, a different style.
avoid: Finance, healthcare, legal, and other products where trust comes first. The clash reads as unserious.
Dense data interfaces. Patterns compete with the content.

fingerprint.note: Saturated panels and shapes cover a noticeable share of the page. Provisional: set from the specimen, recalibrate with measured references.
The colors that appear are strong, not muted.
Repeating laminate-style patterns cover part of the page.

synthesis: Furniture defines the style: Sottsass’s [Carlton](ref:sottsass-carlton-room-divider-1981) and [Casablanca](ref:sottsass-casablanca-sideboard-1981), Shire’s [Bel Air chair](ref:shire-bel-air-chair-1982), and De Lucchi’s [First chair](ref:de-lucchi-first-chair-1983) combine laminate color with toy-like parts.
Pattern is equally central. Du Pasquier’s [Gabon textile](ref:du-pasquier-gabon-textile-1982) and the [1985 swatch card](ref:memphis-printed-cotton-swatch-1985) show the prints that covered surfaces.

Christoph Radl’s [logotype](ref:radl-memphis-logotype-drawing-1982) and [leaflet](ref:radl-memphis-milano-leaflet-1983) show how the group presented itself in print: blocky letters, black grounds, and labelled pattern samples.

Most Memphis references are link-only, because the works are in copyright. The exception is a screenshot of [Abet Laminati’s Bacterio page](ref:abet-bacterio-laminate-page), which shows the laminate pattern still in production. The Memphis Milano company website was captured but not kept: it sells the work but is not itself in the style.

references.title: Bacterio laminate, Abet Laminati product page
references.note: The page calls Bacterio “the iconic pattern of the Memphis movement”. It shows the laminate that covered Memphis furniture surfaces.

references.title: Bel Air chair
references.note: The V&A calls it a signature object of the Memphis collective.

references.title: Carlton room divider
references.note: A founding piece of the 1981 Memphis collection and the group’s best-known object.

references.title: Casablanca sideboard
references.note: Part of the first Memphis collection; its patterned laminate is a direct example of the style’s surface grammar.

references.title: First chair
references.note: Made and sold by Memphis; the Met calls it characteristic of the collective’s designs.

references.title: Gabon textile samples
references.note: Du Pasquier was a Memphis member and a principal pattern designer for the group; this print shows the style’s surface language.

references.title: Memphis logotype drawing
references.note: The group’s own wordmark, drawn by its graphic designer.

references.title: Memphis Milano leaflet
references.note: Official Memphis printed matter by the group’s graphic designer, showing its patterns and products together.

references.title: Memphis printed cotton swatch card
references.note: A Memphis trade sample that joins the group’s printed pattern with its graphic identity.

references.title: Super lamp
references.note: Shown at the first Memphis exhibition in 1981; the V&A calls it iconic.

references.title: Tawaraya colour tests
references.note: A design drawing for one of the defining pieces of the first Memphis exhibition.

references.title: Victoria vase
references.note: Made by Memphis S.R.L., and its stacked forms and clashing colors match the group’s object language.

references.title: View of an Interior
references.note: A print by a Memphis founder that shows the group’s idea of total surface pattern.
